Heat tolerance varies widely across wild Saccharomyces isolates

:::subtitle

We measured growth across a temperature gradient for 84 wild S. cerevisiae strains and found that thermotolerance correlates with the latitude of the strain’s collection site.

::: 

:::abstract

Wild Saccharomyces isolates show striking variation in tolerance to environmental stress, but the extent of variation across natural populations is poorly characterized. We collected 84 strains spanning a latitudinal range from the tropics to the boreal zone and measured growth rates across nine temperatures spanning 12–42 °C.

We found that thermotolerance was strongly correlated with the latitude of the collection site, with tropical strains showing the highest growth rates at temperatures above 37 °C and boreal strains growing best below 20 °C. The data point to local adaptation as the dominant driver of growth-temperature variation in this clade.

::: 

Background and goal

Wild yeast populations show extensive genetic variation that tracks the geography of their natural habitats :ref. Latitudinal clines in thermotolerance have been reported in other microbial taxa :ref, but the magnitude of variation within Saccharomyces cerevisiae and the degree to which local adaptation drives it remain open questions.[a]

Here we measured growth rates across a temperature gradient for 84 wild S. cerevisiae isolates collected from sites spanning a 67-degree latitudinal range. We use the resulting data to test whether thermotolerance tracks collection latitude (:ref{#growth-curves}) and to identify candidate strains for follow-up work on cold-tolerance mechanisms (:ref{#tolerance-clusters}).

The approach

Strain collection

We assembled a panel of 84 wild isolates from field-collected samples contributed by collaborators on four continents (:ref{#strain-list}). Strains were re-streaked to single colonies on YPD agar, genotyped at five marker loci, and frozen as glycerol stocks before assay.

:::meta

:id: strain-list

Representative wild Saccharomyces strains used in this study.

Four representative strains from the full 84-strain panel — the complete strain list with accession numbers and isolation conditions is available in the supplementary spreadsheet. $T_{\mathrm{max}}$ is the highest temperature supporting growth to OD600 ≥ 0.5 within 48 h; across the panel, isolates span 35–42 °C. The viability index is the surviving fraction after a 30 min heat shock at 50 °C relative to the 30 °C control (mean ± s.d., n = 6); cells were recovered on YPD with 5% CO2 and counted as CFU × 106 mL−1 after plating 100 μL per plate. Superscript letters on the viability index denote statistical groups — values that share a letter don't differ significantly (Tukey's HSD, p > 0.05). yWS-014 is the reference strain, with an assembled genome deposited in GenBank; all stocks are held at −80 °C.

::: 

Growth assay

We measured growth at nine temperatures (12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 37, 40, and 42 °C) in biological triplicate. Strains were inoculated to a starting OD₆₀₀ of 0.01 in 200 µL of YPD in 96-well plates, sealed with breathable film, and read on a temperature- controlled plate reader every 15 min for 48 h.

Each panel shows OD₆₀₀ over time for a single temperature condition (12–42 °C). Strains are colored by the latitude of their collection site, from tropical (red) to boreal (blue). At intermediate temperatures (24–32 °C) all strains grow comparably, but the temperature extremes pull the strains apart by origin.

Statistical analysis

We extracted maximum specific growth rate ($\mu_{\text{max}}$) from each growth curve as the maximum slope of the log-transformed OD trace over a sliding two-hour window:

$$

\mu_{\text{max}} = \frac{\ln(\text{OD}_{t_2}) - \ln(\text{OD}_{t_1})}{t_2 - t_1}

$$

We normalized counts of CFUs as $\log(1 + x)$ before correlation analysis to stabilize variance across the dynamic range, and computed Pearson correlations between $\mu_{\text{max}}$ and collection latitude using `pearsonr` from SciPy.

The analysis pipeline is implemented in R. The core summary step looks like this:

```r

library(tidyverse)

library(broom)

growth_data |>

  group_by(strain_id, temperature) |>

  summarize(

    mu_max = max(log(od) - log(lag(od))) / (time - lag(time)),

    .groups = "drop"

  ) |>

  filter(!is.na(mu_max))

```

These functions are all included in the mock-microscopy-tools GitHub repo :ref. We used Mock-pycolor (v12) :ref to style our visualizations prior to manual adjustment in Adobe Illustrator.

The results

Tropical strains grew significantly faster than boreal strains at 42 °C, while boreal strains outperformed tropical strains at 12 °C (:ref{#growth-curves}, A–C). The intermediate-temperature panels show no significant separation by origin.

A UMAP embedding of per-strain growth profiles cleanly separates the strains by climate zone (:ref{#tolerance-clusters}). The boreal cluster is the most distinct; tropical and Mediterranean strains overlap substantially in their intermediate-temperature growth.

Bonus data: A single outlier strain shows unusual cold tolerance

:::details

:::summary

While not part of the main pattern, one strain (SC-B-021) grew faster at 12 °C than any other isolate.

::: 

We isolated SC-B-021 from a Norwegian permafrost sample. Its growth profile is qualitatively different from other boreal strains — it shows a sharp drop in growth rate above 25 °C and a peak at 16 °C, the lowest temperature we tested (:ref{#outlier-strain}).

:::media

:type: image

:id: outlier-strain

:width: 70%

:alt: A growth curve panel showing SC-B-021’s temperature response, with a sharp peak at 16 °C and steep drops on either side.

SC-B-021 has an unusual cold-shifted thermotolerance profile.

Single-strain growth curves across all nine temperature conditions. Note the sharp peak at 16 °C — every other strain peaks at 28–32 °C.

::: 

We’re following up on this strain in a separate study, where we plan to identify the genetic basis of the cold-shifted optimum and test whether it transfers cleanly to a lab strain.

:::

We have also released the assay protocol as an audio walkthrough (:ref{#assay-walkthrough}) and a time-lapse demonstration video (:ref{#colony-timelapse}).
